newsitem.title: THAILAND: Bloated Thai finance sector poised for major trim.
newsitem.headline: Bloated Thai finance sector poised for major trim.

text.p: Thailand's bloated and turmoil-ridden finance and securities sector is poised for a severe shakeout under the weight of prolonged market bearishness and government pressure for the industry's consolidation.
Analysts said Thailand's 91 finance and brokerage firms should be trimmed by half to prepare them for increasing competition, but that corporate culture would impede quick mergers.

"The number is far too many. I think people agree that it should come down by half, but corporate culture is not conducive to mergers. People don't like to lose face or to give up business easily," said Mike Stead of Union Securities Plc.

Finance One Plc, Thailand's biggest finance firm, and Thai Danu Bank Plc on Friday took the first step toward their merger with the blessings of Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan and the Bank of Thailand.

The biggest Thai financial merger came after weeks of rumours that Finance One faced liquidity problems stemming partly from its exposure to the troubled property sector. Its alliance with Thai Danu, which would retain the Thai Danu Bank name, was expected to take six to nine months to materialise.

Amnuay pledged government assistance for future mergers of financial institutions, including help to smooth out tax and legal obstacles and liquidity injection for firms facing cashflow problems during their restructuring.

"Consolidation is essential. The current bust is a lesson for an industry that has not seen downside for 4-5 years. Their past overspending increased the pain of the adjustment they feel now," said Supawat Saichua of Krungthai Thanakit Plc.
Supawat said some Thai brokerage houses had trimmed payrolls by half during the past year while executives of big firms like Phatra Thanakit Plc had taken voluntary pay-cuts.
The finance sector has struggled in the past year under a slowing Thai economy, an extended stock market downturn to near five-year lows, and a rise in non-performing loans.

An analyst at Capital Nomura Securities Plc expected average earnings of 41 listed finance and brokerage firms to contract a further 30 percent this year from a weak 1996, when overall profits declined about 15 percent.

Another analyst at Krungthai Thanakit estimated at least 12 percent of all finance company loans, mostly to the property sector, were non-performing and the ratio was rising. Finance firms lent a quarter of their loans to property developers.
The central bank, in a move to boost the industry, this month ordered 10 finance firms to raise capital and told all bank and finance companies to set aside more provisions for sub-standard assets.

"There was evidence for a shakeout even during the earlier boom. The bust just speeded up the process. I think these firms can operate further for a while but their competitiveness would erode over time," said Stead of Union Securities.
Mergers would benefit both small and big finance companies including those affiliated with banks, he added.
Weera Manakongtreecheep, president of SITCA Investment and Securities Plc, said his firm and six potential allies would oblige the government policy to merge.
However, that would only be done after they got a clearer central bank guideline on whether their new company could undertake a wider scope of business, he added.
